subject: Business
title: Minimum Viable Products
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Minimum Viable Products.

hook.text: Zappos tested online shoe sales with zero inventory — just photos from local stores.

buildup.text: An MVP is the smallest version of a product that tests a real assumption with real users.

discovery.text: The goal isn't a stripped-down product. It's the fastest path to validated learning.

twist.text: Most teams over-build their MVP. If you're not embarrassed by it, you launched too late.

climax.text: Airbnb's MVP was a single webpage with photos of three air mattresses in San Francisco.

punchline.text: Build less. Learn more. Ship embarrassingly small.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of an MVP?
options: To test assumptions with the least effort
To impress investors with a polished product

details.summary: A minimum viable product is the simplest version of a product that validates a core business hypothesis with real users. MVPs are not about building cheap products but about maximizing learning per dollar spent. Dropbox used a video demo, Zappos used manual shoe purchasing from stores.
details.whyItMatters: Building full products without validation wastes months or years on assumptions that may be wrong. MVPs compress the feedback loop from years to weeks, letting founders learn whether the market wants what they are building before committing serious
takeaways: MVPs are the simplest test of whether a core business hypothesis is valid
Maximize learning per dollar invested rather than building the minimum product
Famous MVPs include Dropbox's video, Zappos' manual fulfillment, and Airbnb's air mattresses

faq.question: What is the most common mistake founders make with MVPs?
faq.answer: Building too much. Founders add features thinking users need a complete experience to evaluate the product. The most effective MVPs test one thing, like whether customers will pay, not whether the product is fully functional. Complexity delays learning. Ship the simplest possible test.

faq.question: Are there situations where an MVP approach is inappropriate?
faq.answer: When product failure has safety implications like medical devices or aviation. When brand reputation makes a poor first impression costly. When the minimum viable version still requires massive infrastructure investment. In these cases, more investment before launch is justified.
